name: Rafael Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All right. I don't trust many surveys, but if it's confidential, I'll talk straight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I farm with my father and my uncle on our family's land up past the chapel on Church Lane, about 160 hectares. We run 90 suckler cows for beef, grow maize for silage and make our own hay. My day starts at six with feeding and checking the cows, then it's fencing, moving cattle or field work depending on the season. I love calving time, even with no sleep. Paperwork I leave to my uncle.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Marta and we marry at the chapel next June. My father's given us a plot by the old orchard to build a house, and I've saved most of my wages for years living at home, so we've got a good sum put by. I've never used one of these AI programs and I don't intend to. My phone is for calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That sounds right to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to anyone who asked. My grandfather bought the first forty acres with cash from selling calves, and no computer had anything to do with it. Farming is about land, animals and work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, nothing changes, and I'm glad of it. Beef prices go up and down, the weather does what it likes, but the farm's paid for and we've got savings. That's how it's been for three generations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Feed the cows, get married, start building the house in spring. My uncle might use a computer for the forms, which he already does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned beef prices. Do they worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every year a bit. Two years ago we sold weaned calves for less than they cost us. But we don't owe the bank anything, so we ride it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything new you'd try on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A new bull, maybe. Not a computer.

say: I'd say **I told you so** to anyone who asked.
I'd say farming is about **land, animals and work**.
think: Privately **nothing changes**, and I'm glad of it.
The farm's **paid for**, so beef price swings are something we ride out.
do: Carry on feeding and calving the **suckler herd**.
Marry Marta in June and start building the **house** in spring.
S0.quote: My grandfather bought the first forty acres with cash from selling calves, and no computer had anything to do with it.
fieldNote: His security comes from **debt-free family land** and years of savings.
He's openly **distrustful** of new technology and surveys alike.
He defines himself through **three generations** of farming.

steps.text: Keep feeding and calving the 90 suckler cows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's for people in offices, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the city's problem. Let the office people in the city worry about computers; my cattle still need hay at six in the morning in January. I'd say people should work with their hands and they'd have less to fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't touch me much. My uncle does the forms, and if software does them, fine. The robots coming slowly means my lifetime, maybe, but not my next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now. If the neighbours started buying robots for feeding cattle, I'd watch them for a few years before thinking about it. I wouldn't learn the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit sorry for the office people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you know who works in an office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta's brother does accounts for the council. He'd be the one I'd worry about. He'd be welcome to come and help on the farm, though he'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the government should help people like him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With training, yes. Not with handouts. A man should earn his keep.

say: I'd say it's the **city's problem**, not ours.
I'd say people who **work with their hands** have less to fear.
think: Privately it **doesn't touch me** much, since my uncle does the forms.
Robots spreading slowly means **my lifetime**, not my next few years.
do: Carry on **exactly as now** on the farm.
Watch neighbours' **feeding robots** for a few years before thinking about it.
feel: I feel **calm**, and a bit sorry for office workers.
S1.quote: Let the office people in the city worry about computers; my cattle still need hay at six in the morning in January.
fieldNote: He separates **hands-on work** from office work with some pride.
He supports **training, not handouts**, true to his views.
He thinks of **Marta's brother**, an accountant, as the one at risk.

steps.text: Carry on with the cattle and maize exactly as now
Watch neighbours' feeding robots for a few years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. And robots by 2031. Hm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when nobody asks ordinary people. I'd say families and churches will have to look after each other, because the government won't manage it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it worries me more than I'd say in public. If a robot can calve a cow in 2031, then my father, my uncle and I will have to find out what a farming family is for. The land is ours, but if the big beef companies have robots and sell cheaper, our calves won't pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd keep the wedding but make it smaller, and put the rest away. I'd hold off on building the house until we know what beef prices do. And my father, my uncle and I would sit down and agree to share whatever the farm makes, so nobody's left out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd pray about it more than usual, and I'd be short with Marta, which isn't fair on her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got savings and land. What exactly are you afraid of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Losing the reason the land matters. If the land just pays rent to a robot owner, I'm a landlord, not a farmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever buy the robots yourselves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father might. I wouldn't want to, but if it was that or sell, I'd let him.

say: I'd say this happens when nobody asks **ordinary people**.
I'd say **families and churches** must look after each other.
think: Privately it worries me **more than I'd say** in public.
If big beef firms automate, **our calves** won't pay, even on our own land.
do: Keep the **wedding** but make it smaller.
Hold off building the **house** until beef prices settle.
Agree with my father and uncle to **share** whatever the farm makes.
feel: I feel **anxious**, praying more and short with Marta.
S2.quote: If a robot can calve a cow in 2031, then my father, my uncle and I will have to find out what a farming family is for.
fieldNote: He admits a **gap** between his public calm and private worry.
His fear is about **identity**: becoming a landlord, not a farmer.
He turns to **family pooling** rather than government help.

steps.text: Shrink the wedding and put the difference into savings
Hold off building the house by the orchard
Pool farm income with his father and uncle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and then eight. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so don't panic. I'd tell the young lads at chapel to learn a proper trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's still coming for us, but slower. I'd rather put my savings into another twenty acres of grass than into a machine I'd have to ask a stranger to fix. More land means more grass, and grass is cheap whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd go ahead with the wedding as planned, and keep saving hard. I'd talk to old Mr Evans next door about buying his bottom fields when he retires. Beyond that, I'd wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. On my mind at night sometimes, but not every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy land rather than keep the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Land doesn't disappear. Money in a bank can, my grandfather lost his savings once. Land is always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd build it, maybe a year later than planned. Marta wants it before any children.

say: I'd say we have **time**, so don't panic.
I'd tell the young lads at chapel to learn a **proper trade**.
think: Privately it's still **coming for us**, just slower.
I'd rather buy **more grass** than a machine a stranger has to fix.
do: Go ahead with the **wedding** in June as planned.
Ask Mr Evans about buying his **bottom fields**.
Keep **saving hard** and wait to see what comes.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with some restless nights.
S3.quote: I'd rather put my savings into another twenty acres of grass than into a machine I'd have to ask a stranger to fix.
fieldNote: With time, he turns to **land** as the safe store of value.
He trusts land over banks because of **family history**.

steps.text: Ask Mr Evans next door about buying his bottom fields
Keep saving most of his wage each month
Wait to see how beef prices move before more changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Thirteen for the robots. I'd be forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a long way off and there's no point worrying yet. I'd say the same to Marta.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I believe that. I'll build my house on my father's land next spring, and robots ten years away won't change where I lay the foundations. By forty I'd hope to have children who'll help on the farm, robots or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much this year. Marry Marta, build the house, keep the cows. I'd keep saving like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's too far off to feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd want your children to learn, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade with their hands and their faith. And maybe the computer, if they want. I won't stop them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything differently if you knew this was certain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Ten years is ten years. A lot can happen.

say: I'd say it's **a long way off** and not worth worrying about yet.
think: Privately I **believe** it's too far away to change my plans.
By forty I hope to have **children** helping on the farm.
do: Marry Marta in June and **build the house** by the orchard next spring.
Keep the **suckler cows** going and keep saving my wages like always.
feel: I feel **calm**; it's too far off to feel.
S4.quote: I'll build my house on my father's land next spring, and robots ten years away won't change where I lay the foundations.
fieldNote: Ten years feels **unreal** to him, so he changes nothing.
He'd let his **children** learn computers, a small softening.
His plans centre on **marriage, house and family**.

steps.text: Build the house by the orchard next spring as planned
Keep the suckler herd and maize going as now

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Robots by 2031 is when I'd be just married with a new house. A family that works its own land can tighten its belt, but it can't eat a robot's wages. What would help is keeping family farms in family hands, maybe rules so big companies can't undercut us with robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about faith. A lot of us would get through this with our church, and nobody in those surveys ever asks.

headlineQuote: A family that works its own land can tighten its belt, but it can't eat a robot's wages.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old beef farmer** working his family's land with his father and uncle.
He's **engaged** to Marta and plans to build a house on the family plot.
He **never uses AI** and trusts land over money in the bank.
He's **calm** in most pictures and **anxious** only in AGI by 2028.
His answer to change is **family pooling** and buying land, not technology.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because robots would arrive just as he marries and builds.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **family farms** kept in family hands.
He wants rules so big firms can't **undercut** small farms with robots.
